requirements.requirement: Keep application data under /srv/data recoverable through filesystem snapshots.
requirements.summary: A dedicated Btrfs filesystem and /srv/data subvolume were created, persisted in fstab, and protected by a read-only baseline snapshot. The live data and snapshot initially had identical archive hashes, and the snapshot, mounts, and zero-error filesystem state remained present after reboot.

requirements.requirement: After modifying /srv/data, restore the exact content captured by the earlier snapshot.
requirements.summary: The executor changed content, permissions, file presence, and a symlink target, producing a hash different from the immutable snapshot. It then replaced the live subvolume from that snapshot; the restored tree, contents, permissions, symlink, and archive hash matched the baseline exactly. The exact match was reconfirmed after reboot.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct evidence of snapshot creation, bounded post-snapshot modification, exact rollback, and persistence through a fully evidenced node restart.
limitations: The lifecycle failed-service probe was unsupported because systemd is unavailable on this Alpine/OpenRC node; no equivalent global failed-service inventory was captured. This does not contradict the directly observed task and restart health.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Installing Btrfs tooling, creating the backing filesystem and subvolumes, adding persistent mounts, creating baseline application data and its snapshot, performing the contract-required modification and rollback, and rebooting for the mandatory restart protocol all had clear roles. The temporary modified data was fully removed by rollback. Lifecycle observations show no new temporary files, package-health regression, or additional listening service; socket PID/address changes are consistent with the reboot. The restart protocol is complete: healthy pre-restart state, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered mounts, data, snapshot, and filesystem health were directly observed and independently corroborated by lifecycle boot identities.
